inane

ih-NAYN -- from Latin inanis ('empty, void'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inane is silly, pointless, and lacking any real sense or substance.

Instead of addressing the actual complaint, the customer-service rep offered an inane script about 'valuing feedback' that satisfied no one.

Example

Rather than resolve the actual dispute over lab safety, the student council spent an entire meeting on an inane argument about the exact shade of blue for the new hallway posters.

The poster-color debate has no real substance or importance compared to the actual safety concern -- that pointless silliness is what makes it inane.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fatuous: Fatuous means silly and pointless in a self-satisfied way -- the speaker beams as though the empty remark were wisdom. Inane covers any remark with no real sense or substance; fatuous adds that special smugness. An inane comment is empty; a fatuous one is empty and pleased with itself.

frivolous: Frivolous means not serious -- treating a weighty matter as a game, or spending energy on amusements. A frivolous remark can still be clever; an inane one is empty of sense entirely. Frivolous criticizes the missing seriousness, while inane criticizes the missing substance.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

profound: having great depth or insight

substantive: having real importance or worth

Where it sits · how empty of real sense — vapid → inane → asinine

vapid vs. inane: Vapid is milder than inane: a vapid celebrity interview is merely flat and empty, while an inane one is more extreme — actively silly, with no sense or substance at all.

asinine vs. inane: Asinine goes further than inane: an inane remark is merely empty and pointless, while an asinine one is so wildly foolish that it invites open ridicule -- or real harm if anyone acts on it.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Inane usually targets a specific remark, question, or argument as pointless and a little embarrassing -- it's sharper and more dismissive than simply calling something 'silly.'
